newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian senator's revenge talk threatens bills.
newsitem.headline: Australian senator's revenge talk threatens bills.

text.p: Independent Australian senator Mal Colston, under police investigation over travel fraud allegations and deserted by the government, has threatened political revenge that could wreck government reforms.

Colston, in a series of media interviews, said he would not quit the Senate, parliament's upper house, but would vote against government legislation. The conservative Liberal-National coalition government does not have a Senate majority and has relied on the support of Colston and another independent to pass legislation, including budget bills.
"It just seems to me if my vote is to count, the only way now is to vote against the government," he told The Australian.
Colston's threats come as the Senate prepares to resume sittings on Tuesday, ahead of the release next Tuesday of the government's budget for the year to June 30, 1998.
A Senate motion needs majority support to pass.

If Colston votes with the Labor opposition and other minority parties, and the second independent continues to support Howard's administration, government measures would still be blocked with a 38-38 tied vote.
Colston, who defected from Labor last year to sit as an independent, also said he would quit the deputy presidency.
The government had supported Colston's appointment to the post, which carries extra pay and privileges, sparking accusations from Labor that Howard had bought his Senate vote.
The Senate cannot expel members, but Colston would have to quit parliament if he were charged and convicted of fraud.
